Over the three years of the programme, 34% ($732M) of expenditure is related to activities where performance is linked to the Network Outcomes Contract Key Results Area performance framework and associated Operational Performance Measures. Overall, results indicate that contract teams are, on average, meeting acceptable (or better) standards of contract performance against the key areas. However, 43 instances were observed where a supplier exceeded thresholds in operational performance measures and triggered a performance penalty. Waka Kotahi revised the performance framework in 2020 to move away from a self-assessment model, although operational performance measures which reflect the Contractors’ ability to successfully manage the network, physical works programmes, incident, and customer care remain self -audited. Based on the performance framework results, the performa nce indicates that this component (34%) of the investment, although $78M above budget, can be considered generally efficient. However, the breaches in operational performance measures are potentially indicating a lower level of effectiveness in the underpi nning systems and processes used by Network Outcomes Contract Suppliers to meet requirements. A level of independent supervision on operational performance measures by Waka Kotahi would increase transparency and credibility of this performance framework. Given the declining condition of the State Highways, further consideration is needed to ensure the framework is measuring the right parameters to ensure optimal value for money is realised from this investment. 23 Pavement and surfacing renewal programme delivery performance
Over the three years of the programme, approximately 30% of expenditure is related to pavement and surfacing renewals. Waka Kotahi maintains comprehensive information on this aspect of the investment. A large pavement and surfacing work programme were successfully delivered, achieving 90% of targeted quantities, treating 5,965 lane kilometres, approximately 24% of the network. Whilst the majority (~90%) of the pavement and surfacing renewal outputs were delivered to target quantities across the funding block and recognised by the Review Team as a significant achievement, it was observed that: i. 7% of the targets were ‘not-delivered’ and 3% ‘unapproved14’ work was completed ii. material cost variances from budgets occurred, indicating a level of inefficiency converting agreed investment into delivered outputs. The pavement rehabilitation programme delivered 4% less length and cost 38% more than targeted (resulting in unit costs being 53% more than budgeted). Across the surfacing programme, 7% less was resurfaced than expected at 25% more cost than budgeted correlating to a 35% increase in unit cost. iii. 73% of all works completed were identified as having potential post -construction performance issues (from very minor texture deficiencies through to significant rutting and roughness issues). This equates to a potential contractual refund to Waka Kotahi of approximately $55M, which represents approximately 3% of the total state highway maintenance in vestment over the period. iv. Waka Kotahi also appeared to have deviated somewhat from its treatment intervention strategy with lower classification roads receiving greater quantities of work than proposed in the 2018 - 21 Business Case. PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANATU WAKA IN CONFIDENCE 1 IN CONFIDENCEIN-CONFIDENCE IN-CONFIDENCE Annex 1 Offic e of the Associate Minister of Transport Chair: Cabinet Economic Policy Committee NEW ZEALAND - ASEAN AIR SERVICES AGREEMENT AND PROTOCOL Proposal 1 This paper seeks approval for New Zealand to sign and ratify: •the Air Services Agreement between the Governments of the Member States of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and the Government of New Zealand (“the Agreement”); and •the associated Protocol 1 to the Air Services Agreement between the Governments of the Member States of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and the Government of New Zealand on Third, Fourth and Fifth Freedom Traffic Rights between Parties (“the Protocol”) . Relation to government priorities 2 The signing and ratification of the Agreement and Protocol supports the Government ’s target t o double the value of exports in ten years . Trade, tourism and people- to-people linkages are dependent on the ability of airlines to respond quickly to changing market conditions and to new opportunities. The Agreement and Protocol will provide the opportunity to enhance New Zealand’s international connectivity. 3 The New Zealand Government’s strategic interest in ASEAN aims to foster a politically cohesive, economically integrated, and socially responsible region. This partnership enhances New Zealand’s engagement in ASEAN -led mechanisms, promoting peace, prosperity, and sustainable development. Over the past 45 years, New Zealand- ASEAN trade has grown significantly, from US$133 million in 1975 to nearly NZD$19 billion this year. Executive Summary 4 In September 2023 , New Zealand and the ten members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) concluded the negotiation on an Air Services Agreement and associated Protocol. 5 T he Agreement and Protocol are intended to enhance, and replace , the ten individual air services agreements New Zealand has signed with ASEAN member countries. The replacement treaties create new opportunities for New Zealand and ASEAN airlines. 6 The Protocol was concluded at ASEAN’s request . It specifies the traffic rights that are available to the parties. PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANATU WAKA IN CONFIDENCE 2 IN CONFIDENCEIN-CONFIDENCE IN-CONFIDENCE 7 This outcome is consistent with New Zealand’s long- standing air services policy , i.e., it: •lifts the overall quality of New Zealand’s air services arrangements with the ten ASEAN members ; and •standardises air services provisions such as aviation safety, aviation security and doing business, e.g., provisions relating to opening airline offices, employing staff and repatriating funds , across the ten ASEAN members . 8 The Agreement and Protocol also further enhance the overall New Zealand – ASEAN relationship, given air services are a key enabler of tourism, trade and people- to- people links. 9 The Government has committed to significantly enhancing New Zealand’s priority bilateral relationships in Southeast Asia: Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Viet Nam, as well as with ASEAN generally. 10 An opportunity to formalise and expand these linkages will occur at the ASEAN Transport Ministers’ meeting in Malaysia in November 2024, where a signing ceremony for the Agreement and Protocol has been proposed. 11 As the Agreement and Protocol are multilateral treaties, Cabinet approval is required and they must undergo parliamentary treaty examination in accordance with Standing Order 405. Accordingly, a National Interest Analysis is attached for presentation to the House of Representatives. Background 12 Under an international system dating back to the 1940s, airlines are able to operate international services only where the right to do so has been expressly permitted in a bilateral air services agreement (ASA) or one of the limited number of multilateral agreements. 13 Among other things, ASAs set out the routes airlines may operate , the amount of capacity they are entitled to provide, and the origin/destination of their passenger traffic . Aviation safety and security articles are standard, as are provisions relating to “doing business” matters such as the establishment of local offices , the employment of staff and the repatriation of earnings. 14 New Zealand’s long- standing International Air Transport Policy promotes the negotiation of air services agreement s that will increase New Zealand’s global connectivity. 15 A precondition to negotiating the Agreement was the conclusion of bilateral air services agreements with each of the ten ASEAN members. T his was in order to provide confidence that , in the event o f the Agreement being denounced, the bilateral agreements would be there to fall back on. The precondition was achieved with the signing of an ASA with Myanmar in September 2019 (negotiated in July 2018). 16 In March 2019, the then Ministers of Transport and Foreign Affairs authorised officials: 16.1 to negotiate an ASA with ASEAN representatives , which would seek to raise the overall quality of New Zealand’s air services arrangements with the ASEAN community PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANATU WAKA IN CONFIDENCE 3 IN CONFIDENCEIN-CONFIDENCE IN-CONFIDENCE 16.2 to negotiate the most liberal air services arrangements acceptable to both sides in the event ASEAN was unable to agree to an open skies outcome 16.3 to seek a “ grandfathering provision” in respect of any air services rights New Zealand had already secured with individual ASEAN members that would exceed what ASEAN, as a collective, was willing to exchange, and 16.4 directed officials following the conclusion of the negotiations to report back to Cabinet for authorisation of the ASA text. Analysis 17 The first round of negotiations, in September 2019, resulted in the near completion of the Agreement text. However, three further rounds of negotiations were required to conclude the more contentious aspects centred on the rights that would be available to the airlines of each side. 18 The particular significance and value of the Agreement and Protocol are that they create new opportunities for New Zealand and ASEAN airlines. This includes two key enhancements : (i) allowing no limits on the number of non -stop flights that may be operated by New Zealand and ASEAN carriers ; and (ii) New Zealand airlines gaining increased flexibility to operate flights between ASEAN members and third countries. 19 Taking the Philippines as a representative example: 19.1 New Zealand airlines are currently limited to operating five services per week beyond the Philippines to a single destination in China. 19.2 Under the Protocol, New Zealand airlines will be able to operate an additional seven times per week between a choice of four cities in the Philippines and any destination in a third country. With the exception of Manila, which will stay at seven, such flights at the other three cities will subsequently increase to 14 services per week. 20 21 22 23 19.3 Ai rlines of the Philippines get a similar i ncrease in opportunities when operati ng t o New Ze aland. PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANATŪ WAKA 2 Proposal Feedback Options Proposal 2: Consultation General support for the same public consultation process for all RCAs, including NZTA. Many RCAs felt the consultation requirements were already being met and didn’t need to be prescribed. View expressed by the AA that the 4 -week consultation window is too short; 8 weeks was preferable. As noted above the AA suggested a more prescriptive list of information is included in consultation. The AA also suggested that the Rule should require RCAs to be satisfied with the level of public support before proceeding with changes. Retain as drafted. The draft Rule requires a minimum 4 week consultation, so RCAs could consult over a longer period if they choose. Alternatively, this minimum period could be increased. As noted above, consideration could be given to requiring a more prescriptive list of information being published when speed limit consultation occurs. Or this could be left to NZTA’s guidance. Similarly, expecting RCAs to be satisfied with the level of public support could be considered further for the Rule or guidance. Proposal 3: Variable speed limits outside school gates RCAs and other stakeholder groups provided a lot of comment on the school proposals. RCAs and the AA seemed to want to maintain flexibility for RCAs to work with communities and implement variable speed limit times that works for each school. Some raised the option of permanent or variable speed limits. Existing permanent zones being well supported by communities being cited. Concerns that the definition of outside the school gate does not consider walking routes and will not address congestion, or realise other benefits of active, independent travel to school. Retain as drafted. Allow a more flexible approach to variable speed limit times and distances for each school environment, as well as existing option to activate speed limits for special events outside these times (for example sports event or assembly). This is likely to req uire maintaining the use of electronic signs on main roads. Allow for variable and permanent speed limit changes outside of schools. Proposal 4: Ministerial Speed Objective Some concerns raised over the risk of the Speed Objective interfering with local decision making and that it potentially signalled a less evidence -based approach. Suggestion that the GPS is a better mechanism for the Government to outline its objectives for speed management. Retain as drafted. Remove and leave GPS to signal the Government’s objectives for speed management. PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANATŪ WAKA

Refining the scope and process for speed limit reversals 2 The scope of roads to be considered for reversal has been narrowed from all roads that had speed limits reduced since the Land Transport Rule: Setting of Speed Limits 2017 came into effect, to certain roads with speed limits reduced since Road to Zero came into effect (1 January 2020). 3 The documents now propose to reverse speed limits reduced since 1 January 2020 in the following areas: 3.1 Local streets with permanent 30km/h due to the presence of a school 3.2 Urban connectors (arterial roads) 3.3 rural State highways. 4 The stretch of road outside a school gate will need to meet the new variable speed limit requirements and the streets in the surrounding area will need to reverse to their previous speed limit. 5 Reduced speed limits on arterial roads and rural State highways can only be retained if the Road Controlling Authority (RCA) can demonstrate public support for the lower speed limit. For urban connectors the speed limit for the whole corridor will either be reversed or retained. For rural State highways, the RCA would be able to segment the corridor to consult on retaining reduced speed limits on sections where the topography changes, i.e. segmenting a cor ridor by straight segments and windy, hilly segments . 6 Regarding State highways, we understand your concerns are primarily around speed limits being reduced from 100km/h to 80km/h (or lower) . To capture this we have referred to rural State highways in the draft Rule. This will exclude State highways in urban environments or passing through town centres. 7 The ability to segment rural State highways is not in the draft Rule as it currently stands. We will ensure it is covered off in the Rule prior to lodgement. 8 The RCA will need to undertake consultation in line with the new consultation requirements in the draft Rule. As part of obtaining public support, RCAs can present economic and safety analysis to inform the consultation process, but this is not mandatory (this is not explicitly covered in the Rule, but can be covered in guidance) . 9 The narrowed scope is expected to deliver the reversals that you are expecting. It is also expected to be a less onerous task for RCAs as they will need to identify fewer roads to be considered for reversal . To retain lower speed limits, RCAs will only need PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANATŪ WAKA UNCLASSIFIED UNCLASSIFIED Page 4 of 5 to demonstrate public support rather than the previously proposed criteria of public support, positive economic analysis and a high rate of compliance. Changes to the proposed Ministerial Speed Direction 10 Following our discussion with you, we propose renaming the Ministerial Speed Direction to the Ministerial Speed Objective. This is to reflect our conversation with you about the role of this tool, where you indicated that RCAs should have regard to it, rat her than give effect to. Therefore, the updated draft Rule requires RCAs to have regard to the Ministerial Speed Objective (alongside the Government Policy Statement on land transport) when considering speed limit changes. 11 The change in scope provides more flexibility for RCAs to respond to safety concerns on their network beyond what may be included in the Objective . Any proposed speed limit changes would have to align with the new speed limit classifications in the draft Rule, and be subject to cost benefit analysis and public consultation . Variable speed limits outside marae 12 You asked for more information on speed limit reductions around marae. NZTA has advised there are two marae (Mahimaru and Karepōnia marae) on the State highway network with variable speed limits outside them. They are both on State highway 10 near Awanui i n Northland with a posted speed limit of 80km/h. 13 In both cases, the electronic variable speed limit signs are activated automatically through sensor -pads embedded in the highway and the marae driveways. The sensors can detect when a vehicle is slowing down to turn into the marae. Once activated , the variable speed limit sign will display a 60km/h speed limit so vehicles can turn in and out of the marae safely. The speed limit returns to 80km/h five seconds after a vehicle has left the sensor. 14 Karep ōnia marae also has a manual SMS solution that can be used when people are walking along the road from the marae to the urupa (cemetery) . A designated person can send an SMS to activate the speed limit sign and reduce the speed to 30km/h for 10 minutes. There are limits to who can use this system and how often. This information is set out in a memorandum of understanding between NZTA and t he marae , including : 14.1 Only three users hav e access to the SMS system 14.2 Only six activations per 24 -hour period, each activation lasting ten minutes 14.3 Access to system can be r evoke d if used inappropriately 14.4 NZTA contact details if the system is not working as intended. 15 We have included an image at A nnex One showing where the variable speed limits apply. This is because vehicles are generally slowing down for a give way or stop sign on the side road and can read it. The increased font would substantially increase the size of the sign to the point that it would require two poles and would not be practical in many instances. 19 To enable RCAs to use the existing static sign (not the large signs) we propose to consult on an amendment to introduce default variable speed limit times into the Land Transport Rule (Road User) 2004. The standard drop -off and pick -up times will be in the Rule and reflected in the Road Code. Changing road categories 22 You asked for more information on when or how an RCA can change the categorisation of a road. The NZTA has advised that there are two circumstances where this can occur through: 22.1 Annual revie ws or updates – councils are expected to do an annual review or update to the road or street classification; however, any changes must be aligned with the guidance and is moderated by the NZTA. 22.2 Future network planning – councils may want to plan for longer -term changes to a road or street classification (i.e. a 10 -20 year timeframe), but this would be dependent on RCA investment to support those changes. 23 You also asked for examples of road classifications, we have attached these at Annex Three . Flexibility was sought to work with schools to determine what works best for each school. Some RCAs preferred the option of permanent or variable limits, while some noted the proposed school travel periods are much longer than existing variable speeds (most operate for 55 minutes per day; the draft rule proposed 3 hours to capture variances amo ng schools). Submitters pointed out that the current rule enables schools to “turn on” the lower speed limit for 10 minutes to enable, for example, children to safely get onto buses for school trips, and asked that this be retained. Concerns that the definition of outside the school gate does not consider walking routes and will not address congestion, or realise other benefits of active independent travel to school. 3.a Retain as drafted.Agree / Disagree 3.b Allow for both variable and permanent speed limit changes outside of schools.Agree / Disagree 3.c Provide more flexibility in the setting of variable speed limits outside of schools, for example: •removing the set times for drop off and pick up and allow RCAs to set variable speed limits that suit each school (i.e. by changing the definition of ‘school travel period’ to mean the start and end time of each school day with up to 30 minutes either side of the bell). •enabling electronic or larger static signs on the main road and leave it to RCA discretion to determine what works best for each location. This would mean NZTA would need to develop a larger static sign for use on main roads. •for schools that have electronic signs, enabling lower speed limits to be switched on for 10 minutes outside drop off and pick up times when there is significant activity outside of the school (for example a school assembly or sports event). If you agree to taking a more flexible approach to setting of variable speed limits, the amendment to introduce standard school travel periods into the Land Transport (Road User) Rule 2004 would not be progressed. PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY TE MANATŪ WAKA MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY TE MANATŪ WAKA MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT • The Government intends to appoint a skills -based board (the ALR Board) to transition from the current representative board. The ALR Board will drive the detailed planning phase and transition the project through to a formal legal entity by the end of 2022. That entity will be responsible for overseeing the completion of the detailed planning and the delivery of the project following a final investment decision. • The ALR Board will endure through the phases of the project, continuing to be the responsible board once the new legal entity is created. • As Sponsors, we have agreed in principle that the ALR Board will consist of between five and seven members including a Chair . It also enables a quorum for decision making, which will then be finalised in the Terms of Reference that Sponsoring Ministers have received delegat ion to approve through Cabinet’s decisions in December 2021. Details about these appointments • We intend to make three priority appointments at this stage, with the remaining appointments appointed in the third quarter of 2022. These appointments were prioritised to ensure continuity of knowledge exists, and key leadership roles were identified early , and allow the incoming Chair to shape the direction of the Board. • The Chair will have a very demanding role which will be different and, in many respects, more demanding than other Crown Chairs. The Chair will be the public face of the ALR Project in local communi ties and will need to confidently fro nt and navigate issues in the three very different political environments of central government, Auckland, and iwi in Tāmaki Makaurau. Their ability to personally demonstrate leadership and accountability for the impacts of the ALR Board’s decisions will be necessary to maintain the Project’s credibility and social license throughout its lifecycle. • In addition, the Chair must be able to demonstrate an appreciation of the types of financial, technical, commercial or legal issues, which could be expected to arise from designing and delivering a project of this nature. They will also hold the role of Senior Responsible Officer for the Project at this stage until the final Delivery Entity is formed. • Members of the ALR Board n eed to have a range of technical, policy, commercial and social attributes. Required competencies include significant governance experience of projects of scale and complexity, deep understanding of Te ao Māori, Te Tiriti o Waitangi and engagement with man a whenua and mataawaka in Tāmaki Makaurau, and the ability to operate collaboratively and navigate a politicised environment. Candidate for appointment – Hon Dame Fran Wilde • We intend to appoint Hon Dame Wilde as Chair of the ALR Board. Hon Dame Wilde is a highly experienced director who has served as a Cabinet Minister, Mayor, and in senior governance roles on many significant central and local g overnment boards. • Hon Dame Wi lde’s diverse range of experiences in governance, politics, community involvement, working with iwi, and delivering transport and urban development outcomes meet the requirements we are seeking from the ALR Board Chair.

PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY THE MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANATŪ WAKA Page 40 of 68 Updates Northwest Rapid Transit Update A targeted social media campaign is underway to promote the community information sessions being held at venues across the northwest between Wednesday 28 August 2024 and Wednesday 18 September 2024. This includes Facebook posts about the events as well as promoting a project video on Facebook and LinkedIn. The level of detail provided at the events will be similar to what was in your media release on the project on 4 July 2024 and involves an update on the project and talking through the indicative alignment and station locations. SH1 Papakura to Drury Stage 1A – open ahead of programme As of Thursday 22 August 2024, SH1 Papakura to Drury Stage 1A is now fully open with three lanes open in both directions. The project team scheduled to open southbound on the evening of Sunday 25 August 2024, however great progress was made over the past few weeks and the third lane was opened ahead of programme. The project is now open at 100kph with all lanes running on final design geometry. The team is on track with quality assurance documentation to submit the application for Practical Completion this week – two weeks ahead of the contract completion date. The final running surface layer will be laid in October/November. It has an epoxy component requiring warmer and dryer conditions than asphalt only. Page 10 of 13 [IN CONFIDENCE ] 3 Key updates Atlas Wind update Atlas Wind is an internationally flagged vessel which carries dangerous goods like ammonia within its cargo. We, and the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA), have had significant ongoing safety concerns with this vessel, with numerous deficiencies identified, and the vessel being detained on a number of occasions. Our latest detention of the vessel was on 4 July 2024 during a Port State Control (PSC) Inspection in Dunedin and AMSA detained the vessel on Wednesday 7 August 2024 . The Vanuatu registered Atlas Wind is owned by MOVe Oceans Singapore, which is a wholly owned subsidiary of the New Zealand based company, MOVe Logistics. We have also been discussing our concerns with MOVe. We are pleased to hear that after all of this work the vessel is scheduled to discharge import cargo and then is scheduled to proceed directly to Singapore , around Monday 30 September 2024, to be sold. MOVe is then looking to charter a safer vessel. This shows the importance of maritime inspections and good engagement with other regulators, like AMSA, in managing poor quality vessels round our coast. KiwiRail update Maritime NZ is preparing for an additional I nternational Safety Management verification of KiwiRail’s safety management system , scheduled for the week of Monday 16 September 2024. This audit will look at KiwiRail’s processes, procedures, training, risk management and how it brings on new equipment and familiarises staff. KiwiRail advised that the Aratere was out of service from Saturday 24 August – Tuesday 27 August 2024 for the installation of a new gearbox part, and that the ship’s Classification Society was involved throughout this process. Once the gearbox is fixed this is likely to result in KiwiRail seeking to resume passage through the Tory Channel before the school holidays. The Kaitaki is currently in Singapore for a routine dry dock to carry out scheduled checks and repairs, and is due to return in early October 2024 . This means that the Kaiarahi was the only KiwiRail vessel in operation from Saturday 24 August – Tuesday 27 August 2024.
Page 10 of 13 [IN CONFIDENCE ] Key updates MV Connemara Maritime NZ is continuing to make enquiries about the Cook Strait ferry, MV Connemara , losing power late Thursday 19 September 2024, south of Wellington. The Strait NZ- operated ferry is currently under a detention notice. Over the weekend of 21- 22 September 2024, it moved under its own steam between wharves to unload cargo. It is now located at Glasgow Wharf. The ferry will remain under detention until all conditions are satisfied and Maritime NZ, as the regulator, has assurance about the vessel. To be released from det ention the cause of the power loss must be identified , all repairs need to be made, assurances need to be given by the vessel’s Flag State (Bahamas) and Classification society and these need to be passed on to Maritime NZ , and Maritime NZ will carry out a Port State Control Inspection.

Page 12 of 15 [IN CONFIDENCE ] 3 Key updates Public consultation on recovering the costs of goods management activities at the border Following Cabinet Economic Policy Committee and Cabinet agreement in August 2024, Customs and the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) are now consulting on cost recovery proposals for goods management at New Zealand’s borders. As noted previously, the proposals will lead to some significant cost increases for the maritime sector. Customs and MPI met with representatives of Shipping New Zealand on Monday 16 September 2024, who represent the majority of international shipping companies coming to New Zealand ports. A Maritime NZ representative attended as an observer. The Shipping New Zealand representatives expressed strong opposition to the proposals at the meeting. A particular focus was the proposed new $6,268 fee for commercial ships. Concerns included the potential for New Zealand to become an unattractive destination for major shippers due to rising costs, potentially resulting in a reduction of services with longer periods for getting goods to markets, and the prospect of some of the costs arising from the new fee being passed on to consumers. A further, follow- up meeting with Shipping New Zealand in early October is planned. Customs and MPI are currently planning to provide policy advice to Ministers on the fee proposals in the first quarter of 2025. MyMNZ We are developing ‘MyMNZ’, an online interface to enable far greater, and more efficient, digital interaction with the sector for services and activities we undertake. As a regulator, notifications and enquiries are important sources of information used to inform the delivery of our proactive and reactive work. A key milestone was achieved with a new online event notification form launched in support of the new HSWA designation on ports from 1 July 2024. We are continuing this work to address feedback our stakeholders provided about using our digital channels and services. This includes the need for a consistent and coordinated system to provide a single place to submit or apply for notifications , certifications and licences, provide more transparency about where they are in a process, and reduce the time spent repeating information. We are currently working on the requirements for creating another online form for specific types of notifications, and requirements for making more of our services for recreational craft departing for overseas available onl ine. Having these tools in place will enable a more efficient and effective use of our resources. High quality digital information will both reduce the time spent following up with applicants, and lead to better insights and decision making. Connemara Incident The Connemara lost power at approximately 10.30pm on Thursday 19 September 2024, near Sinclair Head. It was towed back to Pipitea Wharf by the tugs Tapuhi and Tiaki. Maritime NZ will be making preliminary enquiries on Friday 20 September 2024 into what caused the vessel to lose power. Those enquiries will determine its next steps. The vessel will remain alongside until it’s deemed safe to resume operations. In this instance, due to the location of the Connemara, towage vessels out of Wellington were able to assist and bring the vessel back to port. s 9(2)(f)(iv)
Page 12 of 15 [RESTRICTED] 8 Key updates Inaugural New Zealand Seafarer Welfare Council The inaugural New Zealand Seafarer Welfare Council (‘The Council’) meeting was held Monday 19 August 2024 with all member representatives present. The Council is an equal participation of member organisations from government, industry, unions, and service delivery within the seafarer sector. A planning day will be held in November to develop a strategy and associated action plan. This will look at transforming seafarer welfare service delivery and outcomes, in compliance with the Maritime Labour Convention (MLC) requirements. New Zealand Cruise Association Conference On Thursday 15 August 2024, the Director of Maritime NZ attended and presented at the N ew Zealand Cruise Association conference . The focus of her presentation was on the wide range of work Maritime NZ does with and in support of the cruise sector. Areas of interest from participants included work being done to facilitate the availability of alternative fuels and shore power, safety and security. A strong theme of the conference was concern about rising costs with short timelines that make it impossible to build the costs into tickets already sold, increasing debt on a sector already holding high debt from COVID -19. In particular , the current consultation processes proposing increased levies across a range of agencies was having cumulative impact. Customs has recently written to submitters indicating, post -consultation, that because of lowered projections of cruise visits, and higher aviation visits, that levies will have to rise further than originally proposed on cruises. This will likely incr ease frustration markedly, as the sector argue that lower cruise activity in New Zealand is a direct result of high costs. Bio-fouling also was a concern; not so much that it was required, but that there was a need for the sector and government to urgently find ways to safely clean the vessels. Winter cruise has been cancelled this year and cruise is 15% down on last year. The sector is forecasting a further reduction in 2025/26. New Zealand was seen as a safe and high interest location to visit, and there are ships available and more being built, but there was a real sense that the cost and difficulty of doing business here was too high and ships were being directed to other places in the Asia Pacific. Maritime in the Media Sadly there was another fatal incident after a vessel capsized on Saturday 17 August 2024 while crossing the Catlins River bar. One person died as a result of the capsizing, and the other person on the vessel made it safely ashore. Our partners in the water safety sector publicly commented on bar safety risks and skipper responsibilities. Our previously agreed content was used as talking points by Coastguard when they spoke on the capsizing.
Page 12 of 16 [IN CONFIDENCE ] 3 Key updates Maritime NZ Board Stakeholder day in Auckland The Maritime NZ Board (the Board), and Executive Leadership team (ELT) stakeholder engagement day was held in Auckland on Monday 26 August 2024. This initiative is part of the Board’s regular engagement programme, which includes meet ing with stakeholders three times a year in conjunction with the Board’s routine business meetings. Engagement included a breakfast session with senior leaders from the maritime community discussing The future of maritime activity in New Zealand and our collective responsibilities in ensuring a safe, secure, clean, and sustainable maritime sector , a me eting with the Port of Auckland to discuss their strategy and their plans , and a visit to the Auckland Marine Rescue Centre (AMRC), with briefings from Coastguar d NZ, Surf Lifesaving NZ and three recreational craft community grant recipients about their work . We have received extremely positive feedback from stakeholders about the value of these cross sector discussions. Southern Tiare Detention On Wednesday 28 August 2024, during a Port State Control (PSC) Inspection in Timaru, Maritime NZ detained the vessel Southern Tiare. The inspection identified concerns with environmental protection, safety equipment, watch keeping, machinery, general maintenance and failure to effectively implement the Safety Management System. The vessel was released from detention on Sunday 1 September 2024, however, one deficiency concerning watch keeping arrangements remains outstanding and is required to be addressed to the satisfaction of the Flag State (Cook Islands) and Maritime NZ before the vessel can depart. Maritime NZ are currently waiting on information from the vessel’s management regarding this unresolved deficiency. The Southern Tiare is operated by Chatham Islands Shipping Ltd, serving as a vital transport link between the Chatham Islands and New Zealand. The detention and eventual departure delay may disrupt the import and export of goods including fuel and livestock. Manahau Update Tugs commissioned by the operator, Westland Mineral Sands, for the salvage operation, MMA Vision and smaller Kurutai, are now in Westport and the operator and crews are preparing for a salvage attempt over the next few days, as conditions permit. The operator’s plan is for the Manahau to be towed to Nelson Port for repairs. Maritime NZ is actively engaging with the operator to encourage them to update the public about salvage plans and to understand crew welfare needs. We will continue to engage with stakeholders to support the operation. Maritime NZ’s team on the ground in Westport include investigators, public information management, legal and a National On Scene Commander, supported by a Maritime NZ response team in Wellington. Once the Manahau is in a safe port, we will move quickly from a response role to a regulatory role. We continue to publish regular media updates about the Manahau as interest in the barge continues to be high, particularly from West Coast media outlets.

Page 13 of 62 [IN CONFIDENCE] Aviation Project: Consultations with the aviation sector Cabinet paper: New Zealand Air Services Agreement and Protocol (Associate Minister) To lodge: Thursday 19 September 2024 To Committee: Wednesday 25 September 2024 To Cabinet: Monday 30 September 2024 On Time Performance (OTP) We met with Air New Zealand, Qantas, Jetstar and BARNZ to discuss our approach to OTP following our discussion at the officials’ meeting on Monday 16 September. The airlines noted that they already publish their OTPs on their websites and were curious about the purpose of the Ministry’s reporting. The meeting provided an opportunity to work through the revised scope of the initial reporting, and to discuss what data is required. We have asked the airlines to supply the data directly, as this should be the most accurate source (and is consistent with Australian practice to source the data direct). However, we are continuing to explore sourcing data from Airport Coordination Limited (ACL), the company responsible for airport slot co -ordination. We informed the airlines that if we are unable to source data from either the airlines or ACL, we will use the Cirium data (which they are opposed to, because of concerns about its accuracy) to meet our September timeframe. We also discussed the intention to build out the reporting to cover regional and international OTP. We expect to provide you with the revised draft report next week so that it can be published in September. s 9(2)(f)(iv)

Project: Airports (Cost Recovery for Processing of International Passengers) Act 2014 Officials have now concluded the analysis of submissions from the consultation on the establishment of cost recovery regulations under the Airports (Cost Recovery for Processing of International Travellers Act) 2014. The Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), in consultation with the Ministry of Transport, New Zealand Customs Service (Customs) and the Civil Aviation Authority, are now finalising advice to the Minister for Biosecurity, which will include a summary of the submissions received. This advice is expected to be sent to the Minister for Biosecurity on Tuesday 17 September 2024 and will be forwarded to the Ministers of Transport and Customs. Almost all submitters opposed the development of cost recovery regulations, preferring the establishment and ongoing costs for new and restarting airports be funded from MPI and Customs respective Border Processing Levies. However, some submitters indicated that if cost recovery regulations were to be developed, their preference is for these to recover establishment costs only (Option 3B of the consultation). Option 3B is the preferred option for officials. s 9(2)(f)(iv)

Page 14 of 16 [IN CONFIDENCE ] 5.1 Other portfolio Cabinet papers with transport implications Committees Cabinet Economic Policy Committee (ECO) Wednesday 11 September 2024 Recovering the cost of border processing services for travellers The Ministers of Customs and Biosecurity are proposing to present a Cabinet Paper and Cost Recovery Impact Statement (CRIS) on amendments to the Customs and Excise (Border Processing Levy) for consideration at ECO on Wednesday 11 September 2024 and Cabinet on Monday 16 September 2024. The paper contains proposals for amendments to levy rates for recovering the costs of processing international travellers. The proposals include a substantial increase in the levy on arriving cruise ship passengers to recover Customs’ costs incurred in their processing. We have provided comment to Customs that the paper and CRIS would benefit from more evidence on the harms or risks associated with arriving cruise ship passengers, and the effectiveness of the Customs’ interventions to address those harms or risks, to make a stronger case for the increase in the levy. The C abinet Paper and CRIS note that the cruise industry is opposed to the increase and has expressed concerns regarding the cumulative impact of recent increases in Government fees and levies on their businesses. We can confirm that this was a strong theme at the recent New Zealand Cruise Association Conference held on 15 August 2024. Since the initial consultation, Customs have written to submitters on the levy proposals, indicating that because of lowered projections of cruise visits, levies on arriving cruise ship passengers will need to rise further than what was initially proposed in the consultation process. This is likely to increase cruise sector frustration markedly, as the sector is already on record as saying that the lower cruise visit activity is a direct result of high costs. Wednesday 11 September 2024 Biosecurity System Strategy Minister Hoggard has begun Ministerial consultation on the Biosecurity System Strategy package. Consultation will run until Friday 30 August 2024, before proposed ECO lodgement on Thursday 5 September 2024, for consideration on Wednesday 11 September 2024 . The strategy aims to address the policy, operational, and participatory challenges in the functioning of the biosecurity system, and is connected to the Biosecurity Act Amendment Bill proposals. While the proposal does not contain any obvious concerns for the maritime transport system, Maritime NZ has asked the Ministry for Primary Industries to involve us in any future work that touches on our functions such as: • our current approach to Ballast Water Management • the role of Regional Councils/Harbourmasters; and • vessels and those on- board (particularly with regard to safety).
Page 14 of 19 [IN CONFIDENCE ] Manahau response After being refloated on Friday 6 September 2024, the Manahau was towed from Westport to Port Nelson on Sunday 8 September 2024. The barge was towed into Tasman Bay by the offshore vessel MMA Vision with the tug Kurutai in support. The Kurutai and Port Nelson harbour tugs then towed the barge into port. Maritime NZ placed the vessel under detention for safety reasons. Maritime NZ was the lead Government agency for the response. Our role included engaging with the vessel owner and operator, the salvage team, councils and Nelson Harbourmaster to provide expertise and support, and monitor plans for safety and compliance. We were also responsible for implementing the restricted public access areas. Our involvement was misreported in media on several occasions and we wrote to editors to have the record corrected. The cause of the grounding has yet to be identified and Maritime NZ and TAIC are each running separate investigations. The operator has also hired an independent investigator. The Manahau’s repairs will need to be certified by its Classification Society and Flag State (Niue) before it can be released from detention. Maritime NZ will also inspect the vessel and require that any deficiencies found have been repaired satisfactorily before it is released. Maritime NZ maintained reduced restricted access areas around the site where the Manahau grounded for public safety, while the area was remediated. We will formally lift the restrictions once we are advised it is safe to do so. Chatham Islands: supply vessel and Harbourmaster’s Direction An outstanding deficiency on the vessel Southern Tiare (non- compliance with revised watch keeping requirements) , caused the operator, Chatham Islands Shipping Ltd, to raise concerns about the impact of this on vessel operations and the movement of livestock from the I slands. As the Southern Tiare is a foreign flagged vessel Maritime NZ has no jurisdiction in this case and these questions can only be addressed by the Flag State, the Cook Islands . It is the responsibility of the ship owner and operator to ensure that ship, crew, and equipment on board meet the flag state and international requirements that all shipping companies must adhere to. Maritime NZ met with a representative of the Cook Islands to discuss the possibility of a limited transition period to allow the vessel to operate whilst providing the operator time to find the additional crew required. Maritime NZ is now awaiting confirmation from the ship that they are able to meet the flag state’s requirements. Maritime NZ is also seeking a meeting with the Chatham Islands H arbourmaster about a Harbourmasters Direction he has issued that places restrictions on vessels of more than 70 metres length seeking to dock at the main wharf. We are seeking to understand the underpinning risk assessment behind the direction and whether a national control, like a pilotage area, might be more appropriate. We note that, as it stands, the Direction could make it difficult for vessels currently planning to transport livestock from the Islands to do so.

Page 15 of 19 [IN CONFIDENCE ] Maritime NZ media escalation process Maritime NZ maintains a 24/7 duty team, which includes a duty media officer. The duty team is in frequent contact with the Rescue Coordination Centre NZ (RCCNZ), which is staffed 24/7, and has established ways of contacting harbourmasters, councils and emergency services as required. The duty media officer will provide a heads up to your or Minister Brown’s Press Sec retary or Private Sec retary when we are responding to a significant event. This will include information about the event, response, media queries we have received and our approved replies. Examples of when we would do this include major search and rescue incidents coordinated by RCCNZ, high profile recreational craft events , commercial shipping incidents and major pollution spills . We note that Minister Brown retains delegation for Cook Strait ferry issues. Your O ffice can ask Maritime NZ to assist with reactive media lines for queries the Minister might receive. In many cases the work of Maritime NZ is operational in nature and responding to maritime incidents is business as usual for the agency. The Minister’s media role would likely be to acknowledge victims and public concerns, confirm they are being kept informed, provide assurance to the public, state the Government’s established position if there is one, and refer operational questions to Maritime NZ. 3.1 Sector Engagement Engagement with the Fishing Health & Safety Forum On Thursday 5 September 2024 , Maritime NZ met with the New Zealand Fishing Health and Safety Forum , with which we have a long- standing collaborative relationship. The Forum brings together commercial fishing operators and representative organisations to discuss health and safety issues and collaboration opportunities. The Forum also provides Maritime NZ with feedback around the operational impacts of policy and regulatory changes being considered. We had a constructive session with Forum attendees. Two particular topics discussed were how we might further support the sector to provide feedback to us on regulatory proposals, and some new potential collaboration opportunities to address risk. The industry, for example, is concerned about recreational vessels on the West Coast reportedly chasing Bluefin Tuna attracted by large Hoki trawlers. The potential risks with this behaviour is that recreational craft may voyage beyond thei r limits or capabilities and may get too close to the commercial vessel – creating risks to themselves, their craft (and the commercial crew and vessel as well in some inst ances) . We are meeting again with members of the Forum to discuss how we might raise awareness of the risks in this area. Engagement with Bay of Plenty regional Council Senior Maritime NZ staff attended the Bay of Plenty Regional Council Monitoring and Operations Committee meeting on Wednesday 3 September 2024, to outline progress made in national and local maritime incident preparedness since the MV Rena grounding and oil spill in 2011. Deputy Chief Executive for Response, Security and Safety Systems, Graham MacLean, presented councillors with an update on key focus areas that Maritime NZ has worked on to enhance its capabilities for managing complex incidents, particularly in the Bay of Plenty. These included: • updated readiness and response strategies and plans • capability development, including targeted training development and implementation ensuring fit -for-purpose appropriately maintained equipment • Iwi and community and volunteer partnerships • establishment of enhanced specialist support arrangements with both New Zealand and international parties The Council expressed assurance that Maritime NZ has implemented the recommendations of the Simon Murdoch report (2013) and that New Zealand was in a much better position to manage maritime incidents, large and small, into the future.

Page 2 of 4 • The Ministry ’s position on the final proposals is that:
Page 2 of 5 Your early feedback on these indicative priorities, and feedback received during the formal public consultation on the full draft of the GPS later this year will help in the development of the final version of GPS24. The GPS is planned to be finalised by mid- 2023 (a year ahead of Waka Kotahi adopting the next National Land Transport Programme). The National Land Transport Programme is a three- year programme that allocates the National Land Transport Fund to national and regional activities in a way that gives effect to the GPS priorities. How can we ensure we maintain acceptable levels of service with the available funding? The land transport funding system is facing significant pressures due to rising demands and costs. In the shorter term it will be necessary to prioritise effectively and strengthen the focus on value for money. For the longer term, work is underway on the Future of the Revenue System that will consider how we pay for transport 30 to 50 years into the future. The project is a first -principles approach on how the land transport revenue system, might be configured in future to make it more sustainable in our changing context of climate change and increasing cost pressures. This project will take time , and we expect to undertake substantive stakeholder and public engagement . In the meantime, officials will continue to advise Ministers on current land transport revenue settings (including petrol excise duty, road user charges, and Crown contributions) to support delivery of the GPS and the National Land Transport Programme (NLTP) .

Updates on other matters Second Asia Pacific Ministerial Conference on Civil Aviation The second International Civil Aviation Organisation ( ICAO) Asia Pacific Ministerial Conference on Civil Aviation is in India between 11- 13 September. The first conference was held in China in 2018, however due to the Covid- 19 pandemic this will be the first since then. 39 ICAO Member States are in the Asia- Pacific region and expected to participate. New Zealand will be represented by the High Commissioner to India, Mr Patrick Rata. We understand Ministers (or Associate Ministers) from Singapore, Japan, Republic of Korea, Solomon Islands, Micronesia, Fiji, Tonga, Samoa and PNG will be attending. The Conference will discuss issues on regional collaboration, safety and security initiatives, sustainability in the aviation industry, and aviation connectivity. India has emerged as one of the fastest growing aviation markets globally and Indian PM Modi will deliver a keynote address to the conference, signalling that India has elevated this conference in importance. Officials will report back on any significant outcomes from the meeting.

Page 22 of 66 [IN CONFIDENCE] 2 Updates on other matters Department of Internal Affairs’ Regulatory Systems Amendment Bill Amendments The Department of Internal Affairs (the Department) is developing a Regulatory Systems Amendment Bill (RSAB). An RSAB is a vehicle for non -controversial policy changes that improve regulatory systems, and typically includes amendments to several Acts. The Department administers the Commissions of Inquiry Act 1908 (the Act) and is proposing to remove redundant references to the Act through the RSAB. This includes removing the redundant references to the Act in section 9(2) of the Waitara Harbour Act 1940. The Department also proposes to remove the Shipping Act 1987 from Schedule 1 of the Inquiries Act 2013, as the relevant clause in the Shipping Act has been repealed. The Department has assessed the proposals as minor, non- controversial, and contributing to maintaining the regulatory system. The Ministry agrees with this assessment and recommends these references be removed from the legislation. The Department will provide you with a Cabinet paper seeking Cabinet policy decisions in October 2024, with the Bill expected to be introduced into the House in mid- 2025.

Page 25 of 66 [IN CONFIDENCE] 3 Transport stakeholder updates Stakeholder Update CAA Aviation Industry Meeting On Monday 19 August 2024, officials attended the Civil Aviation Authority’s quarterly Aviation Industry Meeting. Meeting attendees included the Tier 1 airports, Air New Zealand and Qantas, industry associations, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, Police and Ministry of Health. A key focus of discussion was on the economic importance of the aviation sector, and the challenges the industry is currently facing with reducing traveller volumes and rising costs. The industry was positive about the work being undertaken by the CAA and AvSec but is feeling under pressure responding to the number and breadth of government consultations. Civil Aviation Rules engagement The Civil Aviation Act 2023 requires all civil aviation rules to be remade to carry over settings in place under the 1990 Act, with any necessary updates to reflect the 2023 Act and other technical changes. Draft revision of all 50 civil aviation rules has been completed. Sector engagement on the realigned rules will be undertaken for eight weeks, from the week starting 2 September until 25 October 2024. We expect to provide the suite of rules for your approval and signature by December 2024. Local Government CEOs Invitation to Address Local Government CEOs on transport policy You received an invitation from Auckland Council CEO Phil Wilson to address a group of local government CEOs (just over half of all regional, city and district council CE’s) in Auckland on Wednesday 11 September 2024. We understand you were unable to accept the invitation. Mr Wilson has queried whether a senior executive from the Ministry can attend instead. The theme suggested by Mr Wilson is “Government policy direction with transport policy, funding and delivery”, though he has indicated flexibility over the topics that are covered. He has noted the intention to release the City/Regional deal framework shortly, and expects the CEOs to participate in a broader discussion about economic development, jobs growth and alignment of infrastructure investment. DCE David Wood has capacity to accept the invitation. As you will appreciate officials can explain government policy, but are bound by convention not to promote policy. If the Ministry does participate in the proceedings, we will provide the Office with an advance draft of the presentation for review and feedback. Page 28 – Chapter 3 Best value for money spent This chapter provides an overview of how procurement ensures that best value for money spent can be obtained when purchasing goods or services to deliver activities approved under s20 of the Land Transport Management Act 2003 (LTMA). This chapter provides guidelines on the:  Identify best value for money at the activity selection stage  Maintain or enhance value for money spent through the procurement process  Financial and non‐financial attributes that are appropriate to value during the procurement process Page 38 – Chapter 4 Strategic approach to procurement This chapter sets out how a strategic approach to procurement will enable an approved organisation more likely to obtain best value for money. The strategic approach has the following steps: 1. Document the policy context (strategic objectives and outcomes, procurement objectives and outcomes, compliance with other relevant policies) 2. Document the procurement programme 3. Document the approved organisation’s understanding of the procurement environment 4. Develop an approach to delivering the work programme 5. Implement the procurement strategy Page 60 – Chapter 5 Supplier selection process The supplier selection process is the means of obtaining the preferred supplier to deliver the outputs based on best value for money principles.

Page 3 of 5 As signalled in the Decarbonising Transport Action Plan , the draft GPS will include a high threshold for investments that are inconsistent with emission reduction objectives . More work (led by the Ministry of Transport) is underway to confirm how this threshold will operate. We are open to feedback on how the emissions -reduction focus is incorporated and communicated to drive the right incentives and outcomes and avoid any unintended consequences. The release of the draft GPS (anticipated in April 2023) will provide another opportunity to provide feedback on this. While the overarching foc us on emissions reduction signals a clear intent from the Government, in practice, it does not mean that every individual investment must reduce emissions. It means that the suite of investments covered by the GPS will reduce emissions as a whole.

Page 3 – What is a business case approach? The business case approach seeks at the earliest stage of the process, to clearly define the problems and contextual state of the district, with engagement of key partners and stakeholders where necessary. The business case approach also seeks to make sure during the lifecycle of a programme or project that the reason for doing it are still sound, and that it has a clear link back to organisational priorities and issues.

Page 31 ‐ We will apply the 'intervention hierarchy' to shape the appropriate mix of interventions for any opportunity or challenges. With our co‐planning and investment partners we need to consider the full range of options to implement the right combination of responses. Our priority will always be to get the most from existing infrastructure and different travel options that are available and avoiding or delaying the need to invest in new infrastructure. The intervention hierarchy is to consider first:  Integrated planning ‐ Plan and develop an integrated land‐use and transport pattern that maximises use of existing network capacity, reduces travel demand and supports transport choice  Then managing demand ‐ Keep people and freight moving and reduce the adverse impacts of transport, such as congestion and emissions at peak times, through demand‐side measures eg supporting mode shift or road pricing  Then make best use of the existing system ‐ through optimised levels of service across networks and public transport services, and allocation of network capacity  Then invest in new infrastructure ‐ Consider investment in new infrastructure, matching the levels of service provided against affordability and realistic need

Page 36 of 68 [IN CONFIDENCE] Updates Southern Corridor Public Private Partnership On Monday 9 September 2024, NZTA officials attended a meeting organised by to discuss a potential public private partnership for the Drury area. It was attended by several developers and a number of senior central and local government agency officials. Mill Road and SH1 Drury to Bombay were mentioned as examples of projects that the private sector would like brought forward. NZTA staff will attend the next workshop, hosted by Kiwi Property, to develop a priority order for infrastructure and financing options for the next five years. Update on Safety Cameras The overall transfer schedule is on track. Transfer of the first Police camera located at Candia Road, Henderson, Auckland has been completed and the camera is now enforcing. Reminder notices have started to be sent to those that have received an infringement but have not paid within 28 days. The next step if the infringement is not paid after the reminder is sent is to transfer the outstanding notice to Ministry of Justice for further action.

Page 38 of 66 [IN CONFIDENCE] Updates NZTA determination made on legality of e- scooter remote operation function This update confirms the verbal update on this matter that we provided to your Office on Monday 19 August 2024. E-scooter company Ario was recently given approval by Auckland Council to operate 150 remotely controllable e- scooters in and around the suburb of New Lynn, Auckland. Globally, these Ario e- scooters are the first share -scheme devices to have remote operation functionality (a person physically removed from the device can drive it via on -board cameras and sensors). NZTA has obtained external legal advice on this matter and has determined that the remote operation of e -scooters without a rider does not fall within the E-S cooter (Declaration Not to be Motor Vehicles) Notice 2023 , or the Land Transport (Road User) Rule 2004 . The law specifies that on such devices (which are defined as a “wheeled recreational device”), the motors are “auxiliary propulsion motors”. When operated remotely the motors are the only source of propulsion, so cannot be considered auxiliary. The effect of the determination is that the remote operation function must be deactivated or simply not used. The devices are otherwise legally compliant and can continue to be used. NZTA is working with officials at Auckland Council and Christchurch City Council, who are c urrently assessing future e- scooter contract providers to ensure a joined- up approach and smooth implementation of the NZTA determination. NZTA does not see this as meaning that this sort of technology could not be considered or used in New Zealand in the future. A wider piece of work will need to be done to ensure safe operations and understand risks and benefits. Ario has written to you seeking a review of this decision. The Ministry of Transport will provide you with further advice. Supporting Motorcycle Awareness Month NZTA is supporting ACC’s Motorcycle Awareness Month in September by promoting the annual injury prevention campaign and sharing relevant safety reminders for riders and drivers via our own internal / external communication channels at no cost. Our latest motorcycling safety advertising is relaunching during the month, and this is funded as part of our National Road Safety Promotion Programme. The activities are planned to take place in September as people on motorcycles are significantly over -represented in deaths and serious injuries on the roads, with a spike in September each year , when many riders return to the roads after winter. Speed Management Plan certifications Under the Land Transport Rule: Setting of Speed Limits 2022 (the current Rule), the Director of Land Transport has a role to approve anomalies in speed limits and specific speed limit decisions made by Road Controlling Authorities (RCAs), as well as to certify speed management plans. Over recent months, the Director has received 34 requests from RCAs to certify speed management plans under the current Rule. Currently any request made by an RCA must be considered and determined by the Director in accordance with the current Rule. With each request NZTA first confirmed with the RCA that it wished to proceed under the current Rule, noting the progress of the proposed Rule and impacts that may have on them when the new rule comes into effect. Page 38 of 67 [IN CONFIDENCE] • The total standard hours for one FTE are 35 hours (this is a standard 40- hour working week minus breaks) . o Over 35 hours per DTO FTE indicates overtime or longer operational hours have been used. o Under 35 hours per DTO FTE indicates operational shrinkage (the time when DTOs are not actively testing). This can be caused for example by DTOs taking holiday or sick leave, DTO training time, or travel time to complete tests outside of a DTO’s home site. • NZTA uses a standard rate for anticipated operational productivity shrinkage of 30 percent . This results in a standard productive range of 25 or higher hours of tests completed per DTO per week.

Page 39 of 66 [IN CONFIDENCE] Release of Quarter 2 Public Attitudes to Road Safety survey The Quarter 2 Public Attitudes to Road Safety survey (covering the period April – June 2024) will be published to the NZTA website on Thursday 5 September 2024. The survey details the results of responses to a broad range of questions focussed on specific road safety topics, including attitudes to enforcement, speed, vehicle safety, impaired driving, distraction, driver fatigue and personal safety. Key findings include: • Public sentiment is in favour of greater Police presence (69%, down 3% on the last survey) and more effort being put into catching people breaking road safety laws (53%), with the latter 4% down on the previous quarterly survey. A total of 48% of those surveyed think that penalties for breaking road safety laws should increase, down 2% on the last survey. • A 5% increase in agreement to the statement ‘someone who drinks and drives is likely to get caught’, up from 37% to 42%. • Most New Zealanders (91%) support lower speed limits (40km/h or lower) around schools in urban areas. Three in five (62%) support lowering speed limits in high-risk areas, with 52% supporting 30km/h speed limits in urban areas generally (not necessarily with schools nearby). These figures are unchanged from the previous survey. • A total of 60% support compulsory roadside drug testing of drivers (down 2% on the previous survey). • Just under half (49%) think safety cameras help to reduce road deaths (up 2% on previous survey); 54% support more safety cameras (down three percent on previous survey); while 68% at least somewhat agree that safety cameras are effective for reducing the number of people driving over the speed limit (down 2% ). The quarterly report has a margin of error of around plus or minus 2.19% based on a sample size of 1,999 (slightly up on the previous quarter of 1,806 respondents). This will be the last quarterly survey, with the frequency now moving to annual. Driver Licensing wait times Summary for week ending Friday 16 August 2024: Wait times for practical testing (restricted and full testing) have improved compared to last week. • full tests down by 11 days (51 days) • restricted tests down by 8 days (63 days) At an individual site level, 20% of full test sites and 10% of restricted test sites met the “30 days or less” target last week. The backlog of tests remains at 72,000 (+/ - 600). While still outside of targets, testing wait times have reduced from last week. The reduction was achieved because VTNZ were able to publish additional testing slots.

Civil Aviation Authority funding review – Release of documents for public consultation The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) funding review consultation will commence from Tuesday 27 August 2024. Two documents are being released: the public consultation document titled ‘Civil Aviation Authority Pricing Review’ and the Cost Recovery Impact Statement (CRIS). CAA costs have not been met by income from fees, levies and charges since 2020 due to a decrease in domestic and international passengers, as well as inflation, changing security standards and other cost pressures. This pricing review focuses on returning CAA to financial self - sustainability by 1 July 2025. The quantum of increases will be a contentious issue for airlines. This concern is likely to be compounded by recent immigration visa fees increases, an increase to the International Visitor Conservation and Tourism Levy, and airport -instigated increases to charges for airlines. The Aviation Industry Association’s Letter on Friday 1 6 August 2024 mentioned the CAA review directly when talking about Immigration NZ. “INZ, like the CAA, largely works on a cost recovery model but it could be argued increases on the scale proposed by Erica Stanford are an over -correction. This is why we must be on guard for the upcoming Funding Review of CAA.” Appendix 3 of the CRIS contains a Ministry -provided price elasticity analysis that indicates that the proposed increase in passenger safety and security levies could lead to a decrease in travel. Specifically, it suggests a drop of approximately 0.33% in international travel and a drop of at least 1.08% in domestic travel based on the low scenario. Guide to Using Autonomous Surface Vessels (ASVs) in New Zealand’s Waters [U NCLASSIFIED] The Ministry of Transport as the lead policy agency for maritime security has led the development of this guidance note, and has approved the final version for publication. The note summarises the statutory responsibilities and relevant enforcement powers of nine government agencies as embodied in three international instruments, eight Acts of Parliament, and 14 separate pieces of secondary legislation. This four -page guidance note is now with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, to be passed onto embassies. We have shared the note with FVEY partners as part of our continuous collaboration with them, and have also used our joining IORIS as an opportunity to share the note with our Pacific partners via the platform.

Page 4 of 5 How should we integrate VKT (Vehicle Kilometr es Travel led) reduction into the development of our Regional Land Transport Plan (RLTP)? The ERP sets a target to reduce total vehicle kilometres travelled (VKT) by our light vehicle fleet by 20 percent (relative to projected growth) by 2035 through improved urban form and providing better travel options, particularly in our largest cities. This target applies to all light vehicles, not j ust those directly powered by fossil fuels. This represents about a one percent reduction in VKT compared to 2019 levels, assuming ongoing population growth and urban development. Later this year, the Government will publish sub- national VKT reduction targets for Tier 1 and 2 urban areas. These proposed targets have been calculated based on each urban area’s ability to reduce VKT, and will add up to ensure we meet the national target. Later in 2023, Waka Kotahi will publish a national plan to outline wha t it will take to reduce VKT by light vehicles in ways that create better cities for people. This will provide a framework for Waka Kotahi to work with councils, i wi, and communities to develop programmes for reducing car dependency and use by improving al ternatives. These programmes for Tier 1 and Tier 2 urban areas will need to be integrated with the RLTPs. While this work is underway, you should consider how any proposed activities in your RLTP could affect VKT by light vehicles. Projects that reduce VK T by light vehicles are more likely to be funded than projects that significantly increase VKT. As signalled through the Indicative Strategic Priorities, GPS 2024 is likely to support councils to invest in activities that reduce car dependency and use, by allocating funding to activities such as improvements to public transport and active travel networks. What does this mean for funding? These indicative priorities signal the overall direction for land transport investment. As with any GPS, any funding of projects or services from the NLTF must be consistent with the direction set through the Strategic Priorities. GPS 2024 will also need to cover other sources of funding that t he Crown may decide to contribute. This includes, for example, Crown contributions to rail, the Climate Emergency Response Fund and the New Zealand Upgrade Programme. This document does not set out projections about available transport investment, including the National Land Transport Fund. This information will be included in the draft GPS.

Page 40 of 66 [IN CONFIDENCE] Update on interventions of note: Overseas conversion testing continues to drive high demand within the system; interventions to reduce this demand are expected to have positive impacts on wait times. We are prioritising work with the Ministry to finalise Cabinet papers to progress legislation changes that enable the extension of the period for drivers on overseas licences from 12 to 18 months before requiring conversion. A VTNZ trial for those converting overseas licences (OVC) commenced on Thursday 1 August 2024 and an additional trial led by the Driving Change Network (DCN) is being scoped. The DCN proposal is for a more intensive support model. Both trials will help understand impactful interventions that can help move people through the system and to inform potential more substantial changes to the graduated driver licencing system in the future. VTNZ have noted that the numbers being referred to the OVC trial are slowly ramping up. Diverting people to the trial is a manual process at the front counter and is a voluntary referral for additional support. Further feedback on the progress of the trial is expected in September 2024. Page 40 of 66 [IN CONFIDENCE] Updates State Highway 3 (SH3) Hydro Road planned maintenance closure State Highway 3 (SH3) between Mangorei and Kent Roads will be under a single lane closure for 7-8 weeks from Monday 2 September 2024 to allow for this 2km stretch of the road to be rebuilt. This will be the first major site of the Taranaki maintenance and operations 2024/25 summer maintenance season. This section of road has proven challenging to work o n safely, despite having a passing lane, due to its narrow width and high traffic volume. NZTA is unable to run the site under contraflow controls due to the width of the road, nor are we able to run stop/go traffic controls during the day due to the high volume of traffic. As a result, we will alternate the single lane closure between both northbound and southbound traffic to accommodate peak traffic flows, being particularly mindful of work commuters and public transport schedules. The road will be closed to southbound traffic between midnight and midday and closed to northbound traffic between midday and midnight. The closures will be clearly signposted so that road users can take alternative routes easily in advance of approaching the site. The alternative state highways are SH3A or SH45. The timeframe for works includes contingency for poor weather and other delays outside our control (such as staff sickness or plant breakdowns). This plan has been developed in consultation with freight and is currently being communicated with key stakeholders and the wider public. Seatbelts advertising campaign NZTA has launched a new road safety campaign focused on encouraging people to wear seatbelts. In 2022, there were 177 deaths and serious injuries (DSIs) in light vehicles (e.g. everyday cars) where people weren’t wearing a seatbelt, and there has been a steady increase in seatbelt -related deaths on our roads since 2020. The campaign has been launched across digital and social channels (TVNZ+, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook) as well as promoted on radio. This is a tactical education campaign for target audiences e.g. 18– 39-year-old males, living in rural areas, aimed at reminding them why they should always wear their seatbelts. The approach is in line with the Government’s new set of objectives and intended actions for road safety that will focus on safer roads, safer drivers and safer vehicles .

Driver Licensing wait times Summary for week ending Friday 9 August July 2024 Wait times for practical testing (restricted and full testing) have increased compared to last week. • full tests up by 19 days (62 days) • restricted tests up by 16 days (71 days) At an individual site level, 14% of full test sites and 6% of restricted test sites met the “30 days or less” target last week. While the monthly backlog increased steadily from October 2023, it has remained consistently at 73K (+/ - 500) since the end of June 2024. Demand for testing has been steady compared to last week, however the increase in wait time metric was due to fewer future testing hours being loaded into the scheduling system and D river Testing Officer (DTO) illness. The amount of scheduled testing varies day to day for several reasons, such as driver testing officer illness and scheduled customer care and staff training. None of these individually are impactful on wait times, but they are, in combination, impactful. V TNZ is continuing to confirm staffing availability and increase available hours where possible (more testing slots were being opened for booking on Tuesday 13 August 2024 which should help mitigate the current issue). Our demand forecasting shows that high wait times will continue, until practical test capacity increases (through meaningful increases to the DTO workforce) to meet demand. We expect to see improvements in early September as the current cohorts of trainees are certified and begin testing.
